transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-07-14
Start: 17:00:00Z
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SE), Samuel Ortiz (HarborMesh - CTO), Priya Nair (HarborMesh - Lead ML Eng), Carlos Mendes (HarborMesh - Infra)
---
Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect):
HarborMesh is building an edge orchestration product that will attach LLMs to routing decisions; they see heavy short-completion workloads (user prompts ~8-40 tokens) plus some longer streaming sessions. Primary goals: maintain p95 latencies under 300ms for short responses in production, and support streaming sessions with p95 under 1.2s while handling burst spikes up to ~1200 concurrent streams. They asked for hosted sandbox benchmarking first; interested in dedicated for predictable throughput but private deployment needed for some customers.
---
Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, uh thanks for taking the time. i'm Jordan with Redwood, AE on the account. Lina's our systems SE, she'll do the bench walkthrough and then we'll talk hosting modes.
[00:18] Samuel: yeah thanks. quick note from me, we have two classes of traffic — very short decision prompts from the edge which are like 8 to 40 tokens, and longer streaming assistant flows for humans. p95 is the big one for us since we need the UI to feel instant.
[00:34] Priya: and hi, im priya. we operate in GCP but a lot of our infra is on-prem for some clients; security is a hard requirement for prod.
[00:46] Lina: cool — thanks. can you give a concrete p95 you want to hit for the short prompts? that helps scope batching and hosting choices.
[00:55] Samuel: our target is p95 < 300ms for the short completions. if that requires dedicated capacity we can discuss costs, but we cant degrade below that.
[01:10] Jordan: 300ms p95 is tight but not impossible for short seqs, especially with prefix/KV caching and continuous batching tuned for small seq lengths. for streaming, what p95 are you looking at?
[01:26] Carlos: for streaming flows we put a soft target at p95 ~1.2s — that's end-to-end chunk delivery to the client. spikes are the pain — we get burst spikes from scheduled processes and customer demos.
[01:38] Lina: okay, so rough convo points: steady-state concurrency, expected peak fanout, and token/sec per instance. do you have concurrency numbers?
[01:47] Priya: typical steady concurrency is ~150 active sessions, peaks can hit 1.2k for short windows (2-8 minutes) during demos. average token/sec per session is small for short, but when streaming it's 20-40 tokens/sec per stream.
[02:05] Jordan: good — that gives us a baseline. for hosted POC, we usually suggest running a token/sec benchmark with your real prompts. we'll provide a spreadsheet and harness. the hosted env will give baseline latency and token/sec across model variants.
[02:20] Samuel: question — how big is the delta between hosted and dedicated for p95? like, is hosted consistently worse?
[02:29] Lina: it depends. hosted has multi-tenant variability but our SLAs and profiling show that for small sequences with prefix caching enabled you can often get within 10-20% of dedicated p95 if you use the right model and batching profile. dedicated gets you deterministic throughput and isolation. private (VPC/on-prem) adds networking and KMS constraints that usually increase p95 by 10-30% unless we collocate GPUs on-prem.
[02:51] Samuel: ok, so hosted might be fine for the POC but prod could need dedicated or private.
[02:56] Priya: also, we have encryption at rest and a customer-managed KMS requirement, plus audit logs for every request. is that supported in hosted?
[03:06] Jordan: hosted supports encryption at rest and SSO but we don't give customer-controlled KMS for shared hosted tiers. for that you'll need either Dedicated with bring-your-own-KMS integrations or Private. we'll send the security docs.
[03:18] Carlos: also curious about cold-starts and streaming p95; do you do KV/prefix warming?
[03:24] Lina: yes, we have prefix caching and we recommend pre-warming for the demos. for streaming we optimize chunk sizes and ordering to reduce first-chunk latency. small model variants with quantization can help too but watch for accuracy regressions.
[03:39] Samuel: speaking of quantization, do you have recommended quant profiles for throughput vs quality? we want to avoid hallucination spikes.
[03:47] Lina: we usually recommend INT8 for throughput-first tests, then run our quality evals; we can show tradeoffs. for some models Q4_0 gives good balance. we can include recommended profiles in the spreadsheet.
[03:59] Jordan: practical next step: we'll send a benchmark template, you'll run the hosted sandbox runs with your prompt set and we'll analyze p95 and tokens/sec. if hosted is insufficient we'll propose dedicated sizing; if KMS/vpc rules block hosted then private.
[04:14] Priya: sounds good. how do you measure p95 — from request start or from first token?
[04:20] Lina: good callout — we report both. p95 latency can be broken down into request-to-first-token, token-to-token timings, and total end-to-end. for UI snappiness you'll care about request-to-first-token p95.
[04:33] Samuel: for our short completions we care about request-to-first-token mostly. for streaming we care about each chunk arrival.
[04:40] Jordan: on concurrency, a design pattern is to keep minimum reserved instances for baseline and allow burst autoscaling; Dedicated gives predictable base capacity and Hosted allows elastic bursts but with less determinism.
[04:53] Carlos: can you talk about batching? if we batch small 8-token requests we might add latency.
[04:59] Lina: continuous batching in our runtime groups tiny requests into micro-batches. for very small seqs there is an optimal batching window — too large and you blow p95, too small and you waste GPU cycles. we can auto-suggest the batch window from your latency traces.
[05:14] Priya: what about token/sec numbers — if we need to support 1.2k concurrent short requests, what aggregate token/sec should we expect?
[05:22] Jordan: rough math: if short requests are ~20 tokens each and peak concurrency 1.2k requests per minute? (brief pause) let's convert — if 1.2k concurrent sessions each do 1 response every 30s, that's 2.4k responses/minute, at 20 tokens that's ~48k tokens/min => 800 tokens/sec sustained during that window. but bursts could be higher.
[05:48] Samuel: ok that feels right, we had back-of-envelope numbers similar. so can your hosted sandbox hit ~800 tokens/sec for short-completion patterns and p95 < 300ms?
[05:59] Lina: likely yes on smaller models and with KV caching; we'll show a matrix (model vs latency vs tokens/sec). the spreadsheet will help identify the model variant and whether dedicated is needed.
[06:09] Carlos: about streaming token rates — will token/sec per GPU differ much from non-streaming?
[06:15] Lina: streaming amortizes differently: you'll see slightly higher per-token overhead because of chunking and more frequent network calls, but overall throughput can be comparable when using optimized chunk sizes. also network egress and client-side handling matter.
[06:28] Priya: can we run a head-to-head: our current infra uses a home-grown runtime; we'd like to run the same prompt set on Redwood hosted, and if possible on a dedicated node to compare. what's the path?
[06:38] Jordan: path is: 1) we provision a short-lived hosted sandbox with an API key, 2) you run the harness we provide, 3) we review results and if you want to proceed we scope dedicated (reserved capacity) including GPU type and QoS. if KMS/VPC is blocking we'll schedule a private deployment discussion.
[06:55] Samuel: timeline — we want POC data in two weeks to present to leadership. is that realistic?
[07:01] Lina: yes, two weeks is realistic if you can run the harness quickly. we'll aim to have the template and sandbox creds within 48 hours.
[07:09] Carlos: for private deployments, how long to stand up a VPC/private control plane?
[07:14] Jordan: private lead time varies — if it's a cloud VPC with BYO KMS it's typically 3-6 weeks; on-prem or air-gapped can be longer. we'll provide a checklist.
[07:25] Priya: ok good. now a few technical details — our requests have a lot of small repeated prefixes, can the KV cache be keyed per-customer and per-prefix to reduce tokens?
[07:36] Lina: yes, you can configure prefix/KV caches and scope them per-customer or per-route. that often drastically reduces compute for repeated patterns. we'll include recommended eviction policies.
[07:48] Samuel: and fallbacks — if dedicated runs out of capacity during a spike, can Redwood route to hosted variants automatically?
[07:56] Jordan: yes, we have smart routing and fallback policies that can route to compatible model variants or to hosted pools; you can set cost or latency-based routing with automatic fallback.
[08:08] Priya: about metrics — we need token-level cost and per-route latency breakdowns in the console for billing/observability. does Redwood provide that?
[08:17] Lina: yes, Console exposes token-level chargebacks, per-route dashboards, and tracing. retention windows vary by plan; we can discuss extended retention as an add-on.
[08:27] Samuel: any potential gotchas we should watch for during the hosted runs?
[08:31] Lina: watch for cold-start variability, overlapping pre-warms, and your network egress from GCP. also, ensure your harness measures request-to-first-token separately. transcription — uh sorry metrics — sometimes our auto transcriptions flip model names; ignore that.
[08:45] (laughter)
[08:47] Jordan: (light) noted. ok let's capture action items.
[08:52] Samuel: quick Q — do you have any public perf data for models under 300ms p95 for short seqs?
[08:59] Lina: we have benchmark summaries and model profiles — we'll share a redacted matrix showing model, sequence length, p95, tokens/sec, and recommended quant. again it's heuristic but helpful.
[09:11] Priya: fantastic. also potential constraint: some customers require region residency in eu-west, will that affect hosted availability?
[09:20] Jordan: hosted has region options but not all models are available in every region. Dedicated/Private gives you control. we'll note that in the follow-up.
[09:30] Carlos: can we get more detail on autoscaling behavior under 2-8 minute bursts? we don't want scale-up delays to cost us p95.
[09:38] Lina: autoscaling can be configured with warm pools and burst capacity; for short bursts we recommend a minimum reserved baseline plus warm standby to absorb spikes. we can show a sizing example in the spreadsheet.
[09:52] Samuel: ok wrapping up — two-week POC, hosted sandbox first, then decide on dedicated if needed. any final notes?
[09:59] Priya: thanks, sounds good. Priya will share prompt set and some traces.
[10:05] Carlos: i'll send infra diagram and KMS requirements.
[10:09] Jordan: we'll send the template and sandbox creds within 48 hours and Lina will prepare the harness.
[10:14] Samuel: great, thanks everyone.
